title: How do we find the median from a table of frequencies?
description: The same family size table has thirty six students, so the median is the average of the eighteenth and nineteenth values. Adding the frequencies one size at a time shows which size holds those two places. Keeko doubts this and picks the middle count of the bottom row.
teaching_notes: One idea: add the frequencies from the smallest size until you reach the middle places, and read off the size that holds them. Watch for students who take the middle frequency as the median.

source: Find the median family size from the same table by adding frequencies.
video_script.why: A child who found the mean from a frequency table now finds the median from the same table without writing out the sorted list.
video_script.substitution: the book's table of family sizes 3 to 10 with frequencies 3, 11, 9, 7, 3, 1, 1, 1
video_script.anchor: the table of family sizes with a frequency under each size
video_script.wrong_move: takes the middle count of the bottom row, 7, as the median; 7 is the frequency of size 6, a count of students and not a family size
video_script.payoff_line: The median family size is five

final_answer.spoken: the median family size is five

never_show: 7 as the median, marked as right
maths_rules: 36 values, so the median is the average of the 18th and 19th values
running totals: size 3 reaches 3; size 4 reaches 3 + 11 = 14; size 5 reaches 14 + 9 = 23
positions 15 to 23 hold size 5, so the 18th and 19th values are both 5
slip: 7 is the frequency of size 6, which counts students and is not a family size
video_script.design: One table all video, with a strip of thirty six boxes below it. Each size fills its stretch of boxes, and the eighteenth and nineteenth boxes are marked. Keeko's wrong idea is to take the middle count as the median.

beats.on_screen: title card From your book; the table of family sizes 3 to 10 with frequencies 3, 11, 9, 7, 3, 1, 1, 1; 36 students

marks.book: the title card From your book appears

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about the median.
<bookmark mark='table'/>The same table shows the family sizes of thirty six students. The bottom row shows how many students have each size.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>What is the median family size of the class?

beats.on_screen: the table and the question stay on the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: a strip of 36 boxes in sorted order, with the table above it

marks.strip: a strip of thirty six empty boxes appears below the table
marks.reach: each size is shown as a coloured stretch whose length is its frequency

narration: <bookmark mark='strip'/>Writing out all thirty six sizes in order would take long.
<bookmark mark='reach'/>The frequencies tell us how far each size reaches in that sorted list.

marks.given: the number of students, the sizes and the frequencies are written

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, thirty six students with family sizes three to ten. The frequencies are three, eleven, nine, seven, three, one, one and one.

beats.on_screen: To find: the median family size

marks.find: the words the median family size are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the median family size.

beats.on_screen: 36 values: median = average of the 18th and 19th values

marks.mid: the 18th and 19th boxes of the strip are marked
marks.pair: the line median = average of the 18th and 19th appears

narration: <bookmark mark='mid'/>Step one, find the middle places.
<bookmark mark='pair'/>There are thirty six values, so the median is the average of the eighteenth and nineteenth values.

beats.on_screen: running totals: size 3 reaches 3; size 4 reaches 3 + 11 = 14; size 5 reaches 14 + 9 = 23

marks.run: the stretch of size 3 fills the first 3 boxes
marks.four: the stretch of size 4 fills up to the 14th box, with 3 + 11 = 14 written
marks.five: the stretch of size 5 fills up to the 23rd box, with 14 + 9 = 23 written

narration: <bookmark mark='run'/>Step two, add the frequencies from the smallest size. Size three reaches the third place.
<bookmark mark='four'/>Size four adds eleven, so it reaches three plus eleven, which is fourteen.
<bookmark mark='five'/>Size five adds nine, so it reaches fourteen plus nine, which is twenty three.

beats.on_screen: positions 15 to 23 hold size 5; the 18th and 19th values are both 5

marks.hold: the boxes from the 15th to the 23rd are lit as size 5

narration: <bookmark mark='hold'/>Step three, size five fills the places from the fifteenth to the twenty third.
<bookmark mark='both'/>The eighteenth and nineteenth places lie inside this stretch, so both values are five.

marks.avg: the two middle values 5 and 5 are added and divided by 2

narration: <bookmark mark='avg'/>Step four, the median is the average of these two values. Add five and five, then divide by two.
<bookmark mark='ans'/>The median family size is five.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the table
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble points at the counts row: the middle count is 7, so the median is 7; the bubble is struck out

marks.doubt: Keeko's bubble shows the median as 7
marks.move: an arrow in the bubble points at the count 7 in the middle of the bottom row
marks.why: the count 7 is lit under size 6 and labelled students
marks.fix: the bubble is struck out and the strip of boxes with the marked places lights up

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks the median is seven.
<bookmark mark='move'/>Keeko picked the count seven from the middle of the bottom row.
<bookmark mark='why'/>But seven is how many students have size six. It is a count of students, not a family size.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>The middle of the counts is not the middle of the students. We must find the middle places first.
